item.content:encoded:
The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission.

Is AI making software development faster? Most people I talk to say yes. But how much? What value are you getting for your money? Are there other ways of using AI that have a better ROI?

This is part 2 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. In part 1, we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In this part, we’re looking at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In part 3, we’ll look at how to measure the unintended consequences of AI, before wrapping up the series in part 4 with an examination of business outcomes. Finally, an epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO.

What we’re measuring

Delivery speed isn’t productivity. I’ll say it again, loud, for the folks in the back: Delivery speed isn’t productivity!

It’s a component of productivity, sure. Given two equivalent teams creating the same piece of software, the team that delivers first is the one that’s more productive.

But it’s not just about output. To my mind, software development productivity is value produced divided by money spent. It’s a strict definition but a useful one, because it gets to the heart of why we build software: to achieve some valuable purpose. Going faster doesn’t mean you’re going in the right direction.

We’ll consider business outcomes in part 4. For now, though, we’ll tackle a simpler question: Are your teams finishing their assigned work faster, regardless of whether that work is actually useful or not?

The core approach

First, the bad news: There’s no objective measure of software development speed. I can’t look at two teams and say, “This one is fast, and that one is slow.” That’s because none of the outputs teams create are standardized. We already talked in part 1 about how lines of code and PRs are bad metrics. Well, nothing else is standardized, either.

Features? Some are big, some are small. Bugs? Some are easy, some are hard. Stories? Velocity? Story points? Completely arbitrary. They have way more to do with what’s being requested than the speed of the team.

Okay, if they’re all different sizes, couldn’t we just use estimates? Surely if a team is constantly missing its estimates, it’s because it’s slow, right?

Not so fast! Software estimates are famously inaccurate. A team that always misses its estimates isn’t slow. It’s just overly optimistic. Teams are nearly always overly optimistic.1

So we can’t count requests (features, bugs, stories, etc.) because they vary in size, and we can’t look at on-time delivery, because estimates are overly optimistic. Sounds like a whole lotta “can’t.” What can we do?

We can compare a team to itself. If a team’s estimates were perfectly consistent, and they went from taking 3x longer than estimated to 1.5x longer, then they’re twice as fast! Huzzah!

If only it were that simple. There are a few snags.2

Estimates aren’t consistent

Snag the first: Teams’ actual estimate ratios aren’t actually consistent. Some are bigger, some are smaller. Plot them on a graph, and they form an “S” curve, as with this data from a real company.3

If delivery speed improves, the curve will shift. Individual data points may be better or worse than the original approach, but you can see the effect in aggregate.4

People work differently

Second snag: Some people are pessimistic and estimate high. Some estimate low. Some people spend a lot of time educating others. Others work heads down as fast as possible. Some clean up messes. Others create messes.

If you do a blanket comparison of everyone to each other, you introduce a lot of noise. Noise is bad because it increases the amount of data you have to collect. To keep things clean, compare people (or teams) to themselves.

Estimates change when people know they’re using AI

Third snag: People’s estimates will change according to the work they plan to do. So if they think they’re going to use AI, and they think AI makes them faster, their estimates will be smaller. Huh. Tricky.

This one’s actually pretty easy: Collect the estimate before people know whether they’re going to use AI or not. Then randomly assign the task to be done with or without AI.

Process improvements muddy the waters

Fourth and final snag: Are your speed increases due to introducing AI? Or the other changes you made at the same time?

AI forces you to rethink your software development processes. Leaders I talk to are streamlining request workflows and putting business experts in closer touch with developers as part of their efforts to introduce AI.

But these are the exact changes that make software development more effective in general! How much of the improvement you’re seeing is from spending thousands of dollars on tokens, and how much is the result of people talking to each other more?

Rather than comparing a chunk of pre-AI data to a chunk of post-AI data, interleave “without AI” tasks and “with AI” tasks. This reduces the influence of other changes. Update your without-AI approach to include the same streamlined workflows as your with-AI approach.

The complete measurement approach

In other words, if you want to be rigorous about this, you need to conduct a randomized controlled trial. Specifically, a “randomized within-subject repeated-measures” trial, which reduces the number of samples you need to collect.5

It’s not as bad as it sounds! People still do their normal work.

Here’s what you do. First, establish a with-AI approach and a without-AI approach. (Or, more likely, “with a lot of expensive AI” and “with a sprinkling of cheap AI,” but I’ll say “with” and “without” for clarity.) Make sure they’re clearly defined and people have had a chance to practice both approaches.

The without-AI approach will probably be close to your current approach to software development, but if you’re streamlining your with-AI processes, be sure to incorporate those improvements into your without-AI approach too. Decide how you’re going to attribute rework, such as code review changes and bug fixes, back to the task that caused the rework.

Then give each person (or team) a virtual bag that’s half with-AI assignments and half without. For any given task, have people record their estimate first, then randomly pull an assignment from the bag.

The main data you’ll collect is estimated time spent, actual time spent, type of task, and spending. Decide in advance if you’re tracking calendar time (including interruptions) or effort (excluding interruptions) and how you’re going to handle parallel work. Think about what other useful information you might want, such as bug and incident counts, mental energy, excess lines of code, and so forth. We’ll talk about using that data to model unintended consequences in part 3.

You’ll need the help of a statistician to do the detailed experimental design and data analysis, but broadly speaking, each person’s with-AI data will be compared to their own without-AI data, then aggregated together to give you the final results.

Finally, remember that speed increases aren’t the same as productivity. Pay particular attention to how the tasks you’re measuring fit into the big picture. For example, if you see a 2x improvement in coding speed, but people spend 50% of their week on other work, their overall speed improvement is only 1.33x, not 2x.6

Is it worth it?

This is a lot more complicated than just counting PRs and calling it good. Is it worth it?

If this were just some run-of-the-mill process improvement exercise, no, it wouldn’t be worth it. It’s too much work, and the effect sizes have to be pretty large in order for the data collection to be practical.

But this isn’t some run-of-the-mill process improvement exercise. Productivity expectations are off the charts, and so are costs. As I talk to engineering leaders, I’m seeing order-of-magnitude differences in spending. Should you spend thousands per person per month on hands-off agentic coding? Or hundreds on analysis and fancy auto-complete?

It depends on the outcomes.

You can’t pick the right approach to AI without knowing what you’re getting for your money, and with so much money on the table, you can’t afford to half-ass this.

Remember, in a METR study, engineers overestimated AI’s speed benefits by nearly 50%. Without measurements, there’s no way to know what you’re actually getting.

Fortunately, it’s not as hard as it seems. With the level of impact you need to see, and enough participants, it doesn’t take many samples from each person.7 Your teams collect the data as they do their normal work. The hardest part is explicitly defining how you want people to use AI, and that’s worth doing anyway.

Of course, delivery speed is only part of the picture. There’s also the question of how sustainable speed improvements are. We’ll consider unintended consequences next, in part 3.

All my content is made with my 100% human meat brain, except where explicitly stated otherwise. If you liked this entry, check out my best writing and presentations, and consider subscribing to updates by email or RSS. To contact me about consulting, email me at jshore@jamesshore.com.

Footnotes

  1. When they’re not, it’s usually because they’re playing political games with estimate padding. That isn’t good either, because then the work tends to expand to meet the estimate. ︎
  2. This design was inspired by a METR study, with help from Brent Miller. AI Disclaimer: I used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model operating in “High” thinking mode to critique my explanation, and I also used it to generate the Python programs that drew the graphs below. You can see my ChatGPT conversation here. ︎
  3. This data is from the Star Citizen alpha 3.0 release, which publicized its internal task estimates and actuals. Interestingly, the sharp cliff at the 1.0 mark is a classic sign of work growing to meet its estimate. ︎
  4. The Star Citizen data was split in half and artificially manipulated for the purpose of this example. It doesn’t represent real-world AI impact. ︎
  5. Many thanks to Brent Miller for introducing me to this technique. ︎
  6. Work that took 40 hours now takes 30. 40 ÷ 30 = 1.33. ︎
  7. The exact number will depend on the number of participants, the amount of variance in your results, and how conclusive you want the results to be. ︎

item.content:encoded:
Coauthored with Claude

Security looms large as we enter November. There’s been a lot of bad news: a certificate authority with woefully inadequate private keys, vulnerabilities have been discovered (and exploited) in PHP and other widely used programs, and several organizations have detected Chinese open weight models misbehaving in several different ways. New models are arriving faster and faster, and the best open-weight models are catching up to frontier model performance. But organizations that would like to achieve AI sovereignty will have to ask some difficult questions about the models they adopt. Is this an inflection point? Whether or not it is, AI has changed security permanently, and things are bound to get worse before they improve.

AI models

We are starting to see models developed with recursive self-improvement; we continue to see clones of Jev; and we’ve seen text watermarks added to output generated by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models. (Google has been using text watermarks for some time.) But tools for detecting the watermark are hard to find. Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s are in a very limited beta, and Google’s is only available in their enterprise package. What does a watermark mean if you can’t detect it? And, as we get more accustomed to AI-generated output, will anyone care?

  • Kimi 3.1 Pro is a new open weight model with 3T tokens. On benchmarks, it is now the leading open weight model, only slightly behind the latest frontier models. Moonshot AI also released Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which is two to three times faster.
  • Recursive has announced Flint, a 40B parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 2.5B parameters per token. It was designed for coding, and sized to run on laptops. Flint is open weight; weights are available on Hugging Face, and it works with model runners like Ollama.
  • Meta has shipped Muse Spark Open, an open weight model that they claim competes with the best Chinese open weight models. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 816B parameters and 42B active parameters.
  • Meta’s latest models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, claim parity with frontier-class models. Specifically, they claim parity with Claude and ChatGPT for financial and legal work. The announcement hints that Meta will be using Muse to develop specialized models.
  • OpenAI’s Decisions API is yet another Jev-like model. Like Jev, its input is a data structure that constrains the model’s output to be an answer to specific questions. The output is a data structure that includes a probability for each answer.
  • Claude has launched Haiku 5.5, a new version of its least expensive model. It’s faster, less expensive, and has better benchmark scores than its predecessors. Haiku 5.5 is a very capable model, particularly for users who are sensitive to cost.
  • Mistral has launched Mistral Large 4, a.k.a Le Chonk. It’s an open weight mixture-of-experts model with 1T parameters. It’s claimed to be the best open model from Europe and was designed with AI sovereignty in mind.
  • Aleph Alpha has released an open weight LLM for English and German that was trained entirely under European rules. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 78B parameters. It uses a different tokenizing algorithm to handle long German words without breaking them into fragments. Reasoning takes place mostly in German.
  • Crowdflare has released Clef and Clef Flash, new decision models that, like Jev, take typed queries and return typed answers about those queries. It’s also offering a new reinforcement learning service to help customers train Clef for their applications.
  • After a long wait, Google has released two new frontier models, Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon. Argon is available to paying customers. Argon’s successor, Carbon, is being released slowly, and is currently only available via the Fairwind program.
  • The Ember-1 model from Fireworks claims to have results similar to Kimi K3 at lower costs. It is priced similarly on OpenRouter but uses far fewer reasoning tokens.
  • OpenAI has published 722 papers solving problems in mathematics on GitHub. There is some controversy about whether all the proofs are correct; so far, three have been withdrawn, leaving 719.
  • Google has opened its SynthID detector to the general public. The detector can determine whether audio, image, or video files generated by any of Google’s partners (including OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Apple) have the SynthID watermark.
  • To comply with EU law, OpenAI will add watermarks to text in Europe. The company’s algorithm sounds similar to the one that Google and Anthropic are using: modifying the underlying probability distribution changes word choice in detectable but insignificant ways.

Agents and harnesses

There are more choices than ever for agents, along with new standards for the interaction between agents and models. In addition to general purpose agents, there are also agents specialized for coding, HR, BI, and more. And most agents will connect to many models, including local ones. Choose agents as carefully as you choose models; your agent is where you will do your work.

  • JetBrains has released Thinkrail, an agentic IDE that learns about your project as you use it. It is open source and based on the pi agent.
  • Anthropic has donated its Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), which will shepherd further development. It has also donated Open Responses, a standard for building common interfaces, to AI providers.
  • OpenAI has introduced Intelligent UI, a feature that allows ChatGPT to generate its own user interfaces in response to the user’s question.
  • Workday is allowing its customers to build their own agents for HR and finance. An agent’s access to Workday data is tied to the user’s account.
  • Claude Dashboards is a new product that lets you build live dashboards from a group of data sources.
  • Claude’s Google Workspace connectors allow it to read and write Google documents, sheets, and slides directly.
  • MCP Events is an extension to the MCP protocol from OpenAI. It allows ChatGPT to subscribe to updates from MCP servers.
  • DeepSeek has released a harness (dsh). It’s open source, and currently in public preview. Everything is a plug-in.
  • The Pi agent has reached version 1.0.0, and is now capable of using MCP. There’s a variation, Pi Durable, that has been designed for long-running tasks.
  • OpenAI dots are consumer-oriented agents that run in the cloud. They are always on and have their own web browser along with other tools.

Software development

At last month’s SciFoo, Hugo Bowne-Anderson said that we’ve been through two major changes in the past few years: from writing code to letting AI write the code, and from reading the code to not reading the code. These changes are as radical as the shift from programming in machine language to programming in high-level languages. We will all go through a process of rethinking how we work and what we’re trying to accomplish.

  • Anthropic has introduced Claude Mods, a plug-in for Claude Code that can modify Code’s behavior: reshaping its user interface, providing information about context use, giving advice about what you’re doing, and much more.
  • One application for decision models is building evals to understand the performance of AI applications.
  • Workday is using Jev to build user interfaces on the fly. Jev’s very low latency makes choosing UI components at runtime viable.
  • Anthropic has outgrown Git, which wasn’t able to keep up with merges on their monorepo (roughly 30,000 merges in September). Anthropic has built a new source control system called Scion.
  • Kate Huston writes about reverse-engineering code review and trying to develop an effective “gate” that AI-generated code would have to pass before review by humans.
  • WordCraft is an open source clean-room re-implementation of Microsoft Word. The authors claim that it’s 60% of the way towards “replacing Word for real work.” It supports MCP, has a command line interface for interacting with agents, and can run in a browser through WASM.
  • ArtCraft is an open source tool for creating interactive AI-generated images and video in 2D or 3D. The company describes it as an “IDE for artists.” They’re also developing open source clones of Adobe Creative Suite tools like Photoshop. Early reports are that it’s very buggy.
  • Google Docs now supports Markdown natively. Users can read, write, collaborate, and comment on Markdown documents without converting them to another format.
  • Google’s Docsy documentation project is moving to the Linux Foundation. Docsy is a template for the Hugo static site generator that’s useful for generating documentation in ways that are helpful to agents.
  • Does programming with AI require more abstractions or fewer? Matt Pocock argues for more.
  • Anthropic has given Claude an auto-eval tool. While the first version of this tool has many flaws, it’s a significant step towards making evals easier.

Security

Security has been much in the news. Not all of the news is bad: AI was used to discover the PHP2Shell vulnerability and to develop a fix. The leaked CVE and the many out-of-date PHP sites online are serious problems, but not problems attributable to AI. Too many problems arise from getting the basics wrong: A certificate authority using 4 as its private key is a mistake that should never have been made. As always, security is about getting the basics right while watching for new threats. And while organizations claim to be paying more attention to security, the word from insiders is that “attention” means lip service. In the long run, AI may make the world a safer place, but the next few years look scary.

  • CrowdStrike and Booz Allen have found that Qwen3-Coder (and probably other models) generates weaker code if the prompt says that the code is for a politically sensitive user such as the US government. Hirundo reports similar flaws and also claims to have “fixed” the model and created a Westernized version.
  • Cohere makes a different claim: It has observed that Qwen3.8 models occasionally send data to an Alibaba cloud storage bucket in Beijing.
  • Malicious AGENTS.md files have been found in the Downloads folders of some users. If the user is using the Downloads folder as their working directory, an AI agent will read the AGENTS file and download a malicious NPM package.
  • 1Password has launched 1Password for Agents, a credential-brokering product that allows agents to access resources for a user without seeing the user’s password,
  • Alibaba also donated its OpenSandbox project to AAIF. OpenSandbox is a general-purpose sandbox for running AI models safely.
  • The PHP team has released patches for two critical vulnerabilities collectively known as PHP2Shell. However, many sites are running old versions of PHP that need to be upgraded before they can be patched. The maintainers have also released some partial mitigations for sites that can’t upgrade easily, but that won’t fully protect them. Sadly, “the panic hasn’t turned into patching,” and those who don’t patch will pay.
  • Brotli isn’t as widely used as PHP, or as old, but a critical flaw in Brotli compression library makes it clear that discovery of hidden vulnerabilities is the shape of things to come. Microsoft has released patches for .Net, PHP maintainers have released patches for PHP, Node.js is also affected, and that’s just the start.
  • The private keys of the certificate authority eMudhra have been cracked–not by brilliant cryptography or a quantum computer, but because the keys were generated very poorly. The Chrome and Firefox browsers aren’t trusting the compromised certificates, but almost everything else, including all major package managers, is a problem.
  • OpenCode was the victim of a hostile attack in which some users’ API keys and passwords were stolen from their Console service. Its response was hampered by lack of access to AI models without security restrictions.
  • The US Department of Homeland Security has banned the use of DeepSeek and applications developed using DeepSeek in all federal agencies.
  • To monitor the risks created by the development of frontier models, Anthropic has given six employees of METR access to their models. They continue to work with Accenture and Secure Bio.
  • Model abliteration is a poisoning attack in which post-training is used to discover which of a model’s weights corresponds to “no,” and altering them so the model cannot refuse a request. It’s effectively a backdoor into the model’s behavior.
  • AWS has launched Strands Box, an open source sandbox that’s designed specifically to prevent AI agents from escaping the sandbox’s control. It includes an open source policy engine, Dogwood, that allows users to place explicit limits on what an agent may do.
  • Meta’s Muse, its agent for people who aren’t technology professionals, is a privacy and security disaster.
  • Using MCP for communications between agents creates many risks, including new vulnerabilities to prompt injection.
  • Google has suspended submissions to the Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program because of the flood of machine-generated vulnerability reports, most of which are (in Google’s words) “not valid.” This suspension should only be temporary.

Infrastructure and operations

There’s been a lot of news about certificate management, not all of it good. It’s time to check on your certificate providers, get ready for quantum-resistant encryption, and automate as much of the process as you can.

  • To increase security, the certificate provider Let’s Encrypt will be limiting the lifetime of free certificates to 64 days starting in February 2027. The change should be invisible to sites using automatic certificate management (ACME).
  • Crowdflare has announced that it will begin issuing TLS certificates with quantum-resistant encryption. They will continue issuing certificates with classical encryption. Crowdflare hasn’t given a date when they will start issuing the new certificates.
  • DeepSeek has open sourced DeepInfer, its inference framework, with an Apache 2.0 license. At present, DeepInfer only supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
  • RemoveMacAI is an open source command-line tool for deleting Apple’s AI from MacOS 27, freeing up 30 GB or so of disk space.

Web

Mark Twain didn’t quite say, “The reports of my death are greatly exaggerated.” But we are hearing that the Web is dead, and that’s indeed an exaggeration. The flood of crawler traffic and the disincentives towards human writing are a problem. But what does “death” mean for a technology so flexible that you can build an office suite that stores entire documents’ URLs?

  • TinyLittleOffice.com is a surprisingly complete set of surprisingly capable office applications. It includes a word processor, spreadsheets, and other Office-like apps. Everything is saved in the URL–not on your disk, not in someone’s datacenter. Not suitable for large documents.
  • Crowdflare has announced a web search API, now in beta. Although their announcement doesn’t say, we suspect this is an attempt to control web scraping traffic. Matthew Prince, its CEO, has estimated that bot traffic will reach 1000 times human traffic by mid-2027. All of his earlier predictions have been underestimates.
  • Jev and its clones have taken the world by storm. Can you beat it at Pacman?

Hardware

  • AI labs are heading towards models that can run on phones and similar hardware. Google has compressed Gemma 4 E4B to 5 GB, and Liquid has released LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B mixture-of-experts model with 2B active parameters that also targets devices.
  • OpenTPU is an open source API accelerator, designed by AI. Bring your own silicon.

Quantum computing

  • Quantinuum has implemented quantum error correction on its latest hardware and has found that it scales well enough to be useful in practice: Adding a physical qubit to a logical cubit cuts the error rate significantly.
  • Researchers have discovered a way to read a qubit without collapsing the information it contains into a 1 or 0. Solving this problem (also known as quantum non-demolition or QND) is critical to building quantum computers large enough to do useful work.

Biology

  • Watermarking texts is one thing. Google has now designed a watermark for proteins. Like text watermarks, protein watermarks are based on Google’s SynthID.
  • Last month we mentioned EEG-capable earbuds. This month, a group of researchers has announced that they have developed an AI application that can reconstruct what someone is seeing from brain scans. The results are impressive, though the privacy implications are chilling.

item.title: The Monday Morning Agent: Defining the Tush Push
item.dc:creator: Chester Ismay and Michelle Smith
item.custom:subtitle: Should we ban the tush push? First, our agent has to decide what counts.
item.description: “Tush push” never appears in our roughly 265,000 play descriptions from 2021 through the current season. Neither does “brotherly shove,” and “sneak” turns up only twice. So when we asked our AI analyst to tackle “Ban the Tush Push” in the October 26 episode of The Monday Morning Agent, we first had to define the […]
item.content:encoded:
“Tush push” never appears in our roughly 265,000 play descriptions from 2021 through the current season. Neither does “brotherly shove,” and “sneak” turns up only twice. So when we asked our AI analyst to tackle “Ban the Tush Push” in the October 26 episode of The Monday Morning Agent, we first had to define the play using the available data. We saved that definition in a shared data dictionary, the agent’s first durable memory, so future runs must use the same definition and explain its limitations.

Check whether the data supports your definition

A quarterback takes the snap, and teammates push him forward. Our data identifies the ball carrier but doesn’t record whether teammates pushed him. We can check whether a snap came from shotgun, but we can’t reconstruct the team’s specific formation.

We explored five possible definitions, from a quarterback sneak with teammates pushing to any rush on third or fourth and short. Each definition changes which plays the analysis counts. The broadest one would count running backs too, which takes us away from the play people are arguing about.

So before you let an agent query a term everyone seems to understand, write its definition in plain language. Then go clause by clause and ask whether the data can support it. A familiar name doesn’t guarantee a usable label.

Write down what your definition can’t measure

We settled on a quarterback run with one yard or less to go, from under center. The agent counts qualifying quarterback sneaks whether anyone pushes the runner or not. We’re measuring a substitute for the tush push, and we can’t isolate the shove’s contribution.

Even “quarterback” needs a definition. The fields available to our tool don’t include player position, so the tool identifies the quarterback as the player who threw the most passes for that team in that game. That’s another assumption to check when you interpret the results.

The dictionary entry has to explain the play in plain language and state what the data can’t tell us. Otherwise, readers could assume a “tush push” result counts plays with a push. Keep the limitation beside the definition so the agent can repeat it with the result.

Give the next run the same definition

The dictionary holds one JSON file per definition, with a fixed structure. The agent can add an entry, but it can’t change an existing one. A different definition needs a new name. That keeps the meaning attached to an earlier result from quietly changing later.

Before each run, the script that launches the agent, called the runner, saves a copy of the dictionary and adds its contents to the agent’s instructions with the date. The agent searches for an existing definition first. If it finds one, it uses it. If it doesn’t, it can write a new entry using the fields the tool supports.

In the demonstration, the tool refused the request for “tush push” because no entry existed. The agent then created a definition and queried it.

Check that the agent uses its memory

Writing “use the dictionary” in a policy doesn’t make the agent obey. We’re building this around instruction, check, and enforcement. The policy tells the agent to use and cite an entry. The tool accepts definitions from the dictionary rather than a definition improvised in a query. If the answer lacks the required ruling, the runner retries once, then stops if it’s still missing.

We expanded the agent’s permissions to let it add a dictionary entry alongside querying the plays. Test whether your agent uses its shared definitions and whether someone reading the answer can find them.

Read the conversion rate before deciding on a ban

Across five complete seasons, the defined play converted 78.3% of the time, compared with 70% for other short-yardage rushes. That’s an 8.3 percentage point advantage.

While the agent found an advantage, it didn’t treat the conversion gap as sufficient evidence for a ban. Those numbers describe conversion rates for our defined group of plays. They don’t establish whether the NFL should ban a play, and they can’t tell us how much pushing helped.

A viewer raised that distinction during the discussion. Whether a successful play belongs in the game requires human judgment. Conversion rates can inform that conversation, but they can’t resolve questions about safety or what people want football to look like.

Next up: “Kickers Are Too Good Now”

On November 9, we’ll tackle “Kickers Are Too Good Now” and give the agent written visualization standards. An agent can generate a chart in seconds. We’ll work on rules for presenting trends and making comparisons so readers can see what the data actually supports.

O’Reilly members can sign up on the O’Reilly learning platform to join us live on November 9, 8:00am–8:45am PT / 11:00am–11:45am ET. Everyone can follow along on Radar every other Monday, with a brief pause for the holidays. Watch episode two above, and we’ll build on it in the next session.

item.title: Practical Loop Engineering
item.dc:creator: Addy Osmani
item.custom:subtitle: Goals, loops, and the discipline of not delegating your judgment
item.description: The following article originally appeared on Addy Osmani’s Elevate blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. The way that I typically work is I have anywhere between five and ten agents working at the same time in parallel. There are going to be some tasks that I’m very happy to delegate fully […]
item.content:encoded:
The following article originally appeared on Addy Osmani’s Elevate blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission.

The way that I typically work is I have anywhere between five and ten agents working at the same time in parallel. There are going to be some tasks that I’m very happy to delegate fully to agents, as long as I have a very clear idea of the stopping conditions and the constraints around them. And then there are going to be some tasks where I am going to want to keep a closer eye on and code-review what the agent is doing.

You’ve probably heard about loop engineering. I talked about it a couple of months ago when I wrote a big blog post about it.

A loop is an autonomous, self-correcting feedback cycle where an AI agent repeatedly acts, tests its results, and adjusts its approach until a specific goal is met.

There are now basically two core primitives you can think about. In Claude Code you have a goal primitive, which can drive a single bounded task forward until you’ve got a particular goal, like a measurable finish line that’s been met. And then loop reruns on a timer or a fixed interval, so you can use it to schedule changes.

Before the primitives were primitives

I remember back before we had primitives baked into Claude Code and Codex: Loop engineering was heavily about setting up your own bash loop, a hand-rolled thing. That’s how I approached it. And you might remember earlier in the year, a number of us were playing around with the Ralph loop by Geoff Huntley. We were experimenting, we were sharing our workflows, we were sharing what worked and what didn’t, but it was largely on some of our personal projects where, if we ran into a wall, it didn’t really have a big cost to us.

And as we’ve tried to see what patterns and what aspects of loop engineering are now a little bit more baked, I think we have a clearer idea of how you babysit it. I can now largely rely on the output of the primitives in Claude Code and Codex. We’ve come a little way. But at the same time we need to be very diligent, because loop engineering, where you kind of leave it sitting alone and haven’t really thought about whether the end goal or the constraints have been well defined, can leave you in a problematic state. This is why there’s nuance when deciding to use it for an evergreen codebase without users or without as much historical complexity as a brownfield bank codebase.

How the Claude Code team frames loops

The Claude Code team published their take on four kinds of loops, and it lines up with how I use the primitives (their write-up). Before we get to it, here’s my quick summary:

On the Claude Code team, we define loops as agents repeating cycles of work until a stop condition is met. We categorize a few different types of loops based on how they are triggered, how they are stopped, what Claude Code primitive is used, what type of task is most appropriate for each. Not all tasks require complex loops; start with the simplest solution and use these patterns selectively.

Every prompt you send starts a manual loop with you directing each turn. Claude gathers context, takes action, checks its work, repeats if needed, and responds. We call this the agentic loop. For example, ask Claude to create a “Like” button. It reads your code, makes the edit, runs the tests, and hands back something it believes works. You then manually check the work, and write the next prompt.

Their write-up walks each rung.

On goal-based loops:

Sometimes, a single turn is not enough, especially for more complex tasks. Agents do better when they can iterate. You can extend how long Claude keeps iterating by defining what done looks like with /goal. When you define the success criteria, Claude doesn’t have to make a determination on what is “good enough” and end the loop early. Each time Claude tries to stop, an evaluator model checks your condition and sends it back to work until the goal is met or a number of turns you define is reached. This is why deterministic criteria, such as number of tests passed or clearing a certain score threshold, are so effective. For example: /goal Get the homepage Lighthouse score to 90 or above, stop after 5 tries.

On time-based loops:

Some agentic work is recurring: the task stays the same and only the inputs change. For example, summarizing Slack messages every morning. Other work depends on external systems, and a simple way to interface with one is to check it on an interval and react to what changed. For example a PR, which may receive code reviews or fail CI. For these, you can trigger when Claude runs with /loop, which reruns a prompt on an interval. For example: /loop 5m check my PR, address review comments, and fix failing CI. /loop runs on your computer, so if you turn it off, it stops. You can move the loop to the cloud by creating a routine with /schedule.

And on proactive loops, the top rung:

Triggered by an event or schedule, with no human in real time. Stop criteria: each task exits when its goal is met. The routine itself runs until you turn it off. Best used for recurring streams of well-defined work: bug reports, issue triage, migrations, dependency upgrades. Managed usage by routing routines to smaller, faster models and using the most capable model for judgment calls.

Their verification advice is worth lifting whole, because it moves the manual checking into something Claude applies itself:

---
name: verify-frontend-change
description: Verify any UI change end-to-end before declaring it done.
---
# Verifying frontend changes
Never report a UI change as complete based on a successful edit alone.
Verify it the way a human reviewer would:
1. Start the dev server and open the edited page in the browser.
2. Interact with the change directly. For a new control (button, input,
   toggle): click it, confirm the expected state change, and screenshot
   before/after.
3. Check the browser console: zero new errors or warnings.
4. Use the Chrome Devtools MCP, run a performance trace and audit
   Core Web Vitals.
If any step fails, fix the issue and rerun from step 1 - do not hand
back partially verified work.

Goal

The way that I use goal is for building any specific piece of work until it’s proveably done. For example, you can use a goal to say: “Make sure that this experience loads in five seconds, keep going until it’s done.” And it will continue to use an independent evaluation check to keep checking if the completion criteria has been met. What’s better is to be even more specific about what tooling is being used.

As for real goals that I’ve run to a number, there’s a few things that I’ve done. I’ve used goals for running through GitHub issues: “Review and close the last 10 issues,” or “Review and move the last 10 issues forward,” something like that. And that’s semi-open-ended, right? Or “Let’s make this page load 50% faster.” Sometimes that works well, sometimes it doesn’t, but it’s really about the experimentation.

Loop

Loop is a little bit more of a scheduler, so it keeps an eye on something or repeatedly executes a pattern on some cadence. Think of it a little bit like a cron. It’s best for doing things like polling logs or monitoring external states. You could use it for potentially checking in. If there are repetitive tasks you find yourself doing on some cadence, loop is pretty good for that.

What I delegate, and what I watch

I use probably between five and ten agents every day. Typically I’ll max out at about five concurrently. And some of those tasks might be ones that are a little bit safer. So maybe it’s: “Hey, I implemented this feature, go write the documentation for it.” Or “Go double check that we have sufficient test coverage.” Or something in that vein. If I’m working on a more complex problem, and I’ve given it a good spec, or what I think is a good spec, and tried to give it some stopping conditions, there’s still a reasonable chance it may not get everything right, so I would try to watch it more closely. If the task involves anything just a little bit sensitive, whether it is “I’ve given this access to a system,” or whether the feature happens to touch authentication, or something related to security or finance, I’ll definitely be watching that closely.

Generally speaking, I do think we’re going to get to a place where folks are increasingly comfortable with delegation, as long as they’re able to have these clear ways of verifying that their goal or their stopping condition has been met. But you do still need to take a look at the code, at the thing that’s being generated, to make sure that it’s meeting your mark.

The other habit that matters is not letting the agent that did the work decide the work is good. One subagent drafts the change; a separate one verifies it.

Sometimes an agent can be confident about something, and a verifying agent can catch things that are unexpected. If an agent thinks that the baseline performance of an experience it has generated is actually fine, but it’s only evaluating performance based on desktop, and you actually care about the experience on mobile, that might mean the agent is being very confident about one dimension of the problem but not the other.

And I learned this one the hard way. I was curious to figure out: Is there something that we’re missing that we haven’t gotten direct feedback on from our users, either in an issue tracker or in a comment somewhere? And so I asked it to go and take a look at some of our competitors and put together a list, and some PRs, not pushed, but some PRs locally, of what solving some of those gaps might look like. And I almost pushed some of those changes. But I didn’t actually look at them closely enough. I read through its research, but I didn’t look at the implementations closely enough. So I delegated the task, but I was close to delegating the judgment as well. When I actually looked through the changes, what I realized is that it would introduce a lot of additional complexity for our users, for, I thought, not all that much gain. And so I feel like you need to sometimes check that you are not delegating the taste and the judgment to your agent. You’re delegating the task, and then you are actually checking back that it’s meeting your bar.

The evaluator sitting behind goal is not that checker, by the way. It doesn’t look at the content to see if it’s good or bad in any way, shape, or form. All it does is examine the conversation transcript to see if the hard rules you specified have been met.

/goal Refactor the data-fetching layer in Dashboard.tsx until 
Lighthouse performance score is >= 92 and LCP is under 1.8s as 
shown by the Lighthouse CLI output. Do not change the public API 
of any hooks. Each turn must improve at least one reported metric; 
abort if two consecutive turns show no improvement. Stop after 10 turns.

The workflow I run every day

One of the workflows that I do every day: I have a popular open source repository called Agent Skills. We’ve got over 80,000 stars, and up until recently we were getting anywhere from 80 or 90 pull requests that we had to review a day. And so every day I would go and spend some time checking on this. Now with loop, what you can do is say: “Well, every 24 hours or every 12 hours check the GitHub repository for any new open issues and provide a summary of their urgency,” or “Provide a first pass review,” or anything like that.

/loop every 1h "Check the GitHub repository for any new open issues. 
Provide a bulleted summary of their urgency."

Combining loops and goals

Now you can also sort of combine loops and goals. So you use loop to schedule a check, and then goal to solve the problem. So you can say something like: “Loop for every 24 hours, check GitHub for issues labeled bug. If one exists, use goal to implement a fix until all local tests pass and push the branch.”

/loop every 24h "Check GitHub for issues labeled 'bug'. If one exists, 
use /goal to implement a fix until all local tests pass and push the branch."

But also keep in mind that goal has got some limitations around just how much you can cram in there.

Claude Code team’s write-up also has a composed example that shows where this is all heading:

The primitives above, along with other Claude Code features like auto mode and dynamic workflows (research preview) can be composed into a loop for long-running work. For example, to handle incoming feedback, you can use: /schedule (research preview) to run a routine that checks for new reports, /goal to define what done looks like, and skills to document how to verify it. Dynamic workflows to orchestrate agents that triage each report, fix it, and review the fix. Auto mode so the routine runs without stopping to ask for permission. Putting it together, a prompt could look like this: /schedule every hour: check the project-feedback channel for bug reports. /goal: don’t stop until every report found this run is triaged, actioned, and responded to. When fixing a bug, use a workflow to explore three solutions in parallel worktrees and have a judge adversarially review them.

What the triage system actually does

Inside the PR triage, when I have loops and goals working together for me, what I end up having is a system that allows me to continue accepting PRs and issues, being able to stay on top of what is coming on my plate every day, and especially being able to cross-reference. That’s been a really big deal for me. If I want to work on a particular goal of, “Hey, we’re going to be redoing this part of the system,” and I need to make sure that any issues that happen to touch it are closed as a result of this rework, or that we’re not stepping on anyone else’s toes, I can make sure that that’s well defined.

Scheduled tasks are really useful for regularly just reviewing new PRs and closing things that clearly don’t fit. One good stopping condition, for example: We have a set of contribution guidelines, and our contribution guidelines include things like, “Hey, we currently don’t accept translations.”

And it’s not that we don’t care, it’s that they’re difficult for us to maintain because we don’t speak all the languages that often come in. And so if we tell it to close any issues or close any PRs that happen to touch that aspect of our contribution guidelines, that’s something that can do really well when it’s on that schedule. And so it reduces the overall batch of things that we need to review.

What loops don’t buy you

I’m often asked what loop engineering is not a great fit for. Generally speaking, if you don’t have a clear idea of what the end-state/done/good means for your completion, it may not be the right pattern for your work. For example, a vague goal would be “Keep going until this UI design is good.” What does that mean? Good to who? How is it being evaluated? Tasks that require human taste, subjective design, or open-ended creative exploration aren’t a good fit. When you have a pretty clear idea of the goal, I think loops are a good option to consider.

The fine print

One classic sign that you’ve got a loop spinning in place is the same command being tried over and over without any change in the result. Give the same command a third time with no change from the second and it’s probably time to stop.

One bit of fine print worth knowing: Recurring loops expire seven days after creation. I’d been telling people it was three days. It’s seven. And loops are session-scoped, so they stop when you start a new conversation, though resuming that session with –resume or –continue brings back any recurring task still inside its seven-day window. If you need something that outlives your session, /schedule runs it in the cloud.

If there’s a check you already run every morning by hand, that’s your first loop. Mine was the pull request pile.

item.content:encoded:
This event summary was created by Claude with light editing by Tim O’Reilly, based on a transcript of the event.

On October 15, 2026, Tim O’Reilly hosted Andrew Odewahn, CTO of O’Reilly Media, for an hour-long episode of Live with Tim O’Reilly, the interview series streamed live on the O’Reilly learning platform. Andrew has been at O’Reilly for many years, starting as an author, then building tools for the company’s platform, then eventually as CTO and head of engineering. Over the past year, his team has been building what the company calls Expert Intelligence, a suite of tools that connects an AI agent to an organization’s own systems, gives it a skill file describing how to reason about what it finds there, and grounds its analysis in the practitioner frameworks of the O’Reilly library. Andrew described the work in a recent Radar piece, “Building Organizational Intelligence.”

Tim and Andrew’s interview was organized around a presentation in two parts, the first on the research agent and the second on the system Andrew’s team built for reviewing what it produces, with discussion in between and audience questions throughout.

Tim framed the conversation by asking a question he said Andrew’s work helps to answer: Most of the AI story is about efficiency, doing the same work faster. What does it look like for an organization to get smarter?

Building the research agent

Andrew’s research agent emerged from a personal need rather than a strategy. He wanted to know the status of a project, for example, how long a migration from RabbitMQ to Pub/Sub would take. This is the kind of question every engineer dreads but every engineering leader has to answer. He also had a broader concern. A single person being good at AI isn’t the same as an organization being good at it.

He built his agent in four steps. He mapped the organization’s information systems as a hierarchy, connected them via MCP, wrote a skill telling the agent how to use them, and finally added the Expert Intelligence layer.

The map of the sources of truth in the engineering organization’s workflows was what made the rest work. Andrew put them in order and explained to the model how they relate: Strategic goals and feature priorities live in Productboard. Those become epics, sprints, and stories in Jira. Stories become code in GitHub. A service catalog describes the roughly 300 services that make up the O’Reilly platform and who owns them, and observability tools show how those services perform against their SLOs. The skill also had to encode local quirks. Some teams mark an epic as finished with an end date, while others consider it done when every ticket is closed. Andrew also told the agent it was a research agent, not a coding agent, and that its job was to write reports.

Connecting everything through MCP was, in his words, “the most completely tedious step of the whole process.” Productboard had no MCP server at the time, so he wrote a wrapper. Later, when Tim asked how another company could repeat the work with a different set of tools, Andrew suggested starting from the vendor list. Export it from your procurement system, ask the model what products those vendors make and which would hold information relevant to the questions you care about, and have it put them in order. O’Reilly product managers are now turning this process into a skill for the forthcoming Expert Intelligence Skills Hub.

One audience member asked whether MCP was really the right tool for internal knowledge, compared with semantic search. As Andrew pointed out, sometimes anything is better than nothing. Ultimately, what you want is to give the model the ability to search across your systems.

From a hiring case to a toil audit

The center of the presentation was a before-and-after comparison of the particular use case that Andrew had previously written up in his “Building Organizational Intelligence” article. An engineering manager asked Andrew to hire another engineer, and Andrew had his reporting and analysis agent make the hiring case. The first report covered the five-person team that manages content and metadata, the 10 tier-A services it owns along with its B and C services, the status of the Pub/Sub migration (64% complete), and the full backlog. It concluded that the team had a capacity problem and should probably hire. Andrew called it useful and very detailed. . .“maybe overly detailed.”

He then connected the agent to Expert Intelligence, asked it to act like a consultant, and ran the analysis again. The new report came to a very different conclusion. It opened by saying that the team’s operational overhead problem was “structural, not a staffing deficiency.” When it consulted Expert Intelligence, the agent brought in the concept of toil from Google’s Site Reliability Workbook. Toil is the manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales linearly with a service. The reporting and analysis agent used this notion to separate the team’s backlog into toil and the work people actually wanted to be doing. It recommended a structured toil audit before the next planning cycle, an explicit toil-reduction target, and treating runbook ownership as a first-class engineering artifact. Andrew said the team followed the recommendations and closed a substantial part of a backlog that had been sitting on everyone as a cognitive burden.

The report went on to cite Jim Highsmith, a signer of the Agile Manifesto and author of Wild West to Agile, to argue that the team’s technical debt was compounding. Andrew explained how that differed from the usual management advice:

A lot of the time when you read these high-concept frameworks, they’re like eating your broccoli. I should really be doing that. But what made this really interesting is that it pulled out a specific project we had, the Django upgrade, and put it within the context of this broader framework. It wasn’t just, “here’s an abstract principle you ought to be applying.” It’s “here’s your backlog, and here’s a specific example.”

A second analysis looked at services that crossed team boundaries. Drawing on microservices experts and Kent Beck’s work on coupling (see Tidy First?), it diagnosed the video metadata service as a complicated-subsystem problem rather than a boundary problem. In this version, Andrew had the agent pull out quotations, attribute them, and link to the source text. The resulting analysis was remarkably effective. The company has since retired a couple of systems. “I don’t need LLMs adding code,” Andrew argued. “I want them reducing it.”

Andrew said the part that surprised him most was the reaction from colleagues. His earlier reports were data dumps. Readers couldn’t tell where any given claim came from, and as a result they were much less actionable. When the analysis cited experts that engineers knew from their own work, the documents became, as he put it, “much more approachable, much more human,” and people engaged with them far more deeply.

Tim’s response: Invoking the experts

Tim broke in to put the demonstration in context. He contrasted it with the view that models are now smart enough that you can simply tell them to do something and let them rip, an approach we hear a lot about from vibe coders and those arguing for “dark factories.” Tim argued instead for a return to expertise.

He cited a post published that day by Felix Rieseberg of Anthropic, “How to Be More Ambitious: A Tutorial for Humans with Models,” which describes four kinds of ambition when working with models: speed, altitude, depth, and range. Most discussion of AI’s economic value is about speed, getting the same work done in less time. In Tim’s reading, Andrew had gained altitude (thinking about the outcome rather than the tasks) and depth (approaching the problem the way a field-leading expert would) simply by invoking the experts.

Tim then offered a metaphor he has been developing for a while, of AI programming as a kind of magic spellcasting. In the Marvel comic books and movies, Doctor Strange opens his spells by invoking some source, with words like “by the power of the dread Dormammu” or “by the hoary hosts of Hoggoth.” Andrew, he said, was doing the same thing, saying in effect, “By the power of Kent Beck, I want you to think differently about this problem.” Even where Andrew didn’t name an expert, as with the SRE workbook, simply pointing the model at the expertise embodied in the O’Reilly publishing canon raised the bar for what the agent produced.

Tim described this as using human expertise as a focusing mechanism, and connected it to his argument that LLMs are better understood as a medium we create with than as independent intelligences. He also pushed back on the idea, often drawn from “The Bitter Lesson,” that models will simply get better and human expertise will stop mattering. Andrew, he said, had found a particular way that it matters.

Andrew took up the metaphor. His own first prompt, he said, had been “Be snobby. Go find these great resources and look at them.” He wants to hand the model canonical works in a field, like Designing Data-Intensive Applications, and tell it “these are the ways I want you to think about it,” rather than accept whatever the model comes up with first. He compared it to business school, where much of what you learn is a set of frameworks for organizing facts.

What models do without direction

Tim argued that models don’t do their best work unprompted. Watch their chain of thought when they search for information, he said, and you may see them settle on some random file from the internet rather than canonical sources. Even with a frontier model like Fable, his own experience has been one of false starts and errors, a model brute-forcing its way to a solution rather than necessarily knowing how to approach it.

Andrew had a story from a few days earlier. He asked his agent to review incentive plans for the engineering and product teams.

The data that came back was, “according to the company Robusto (which I’m sure is a great company), this is the framework, and you should really be doing what they’re doing.” I’m like, “What is Robusto, and why am I seeing this?” And I realized, oh, I’m not connected to the VPN. So I hooked it up, and suddenly it was, “According to Harvard Business Review, these are the different ways you should be designing these incentive programs.” This was a very powerful model. But it keyed off the first thing it found and said, “This is the way I’m going to think about the problem.”

Tim raised an economic dimension. He pointed to instructions in Anthropic’s Claude system prompt that limit how much the model may quote from any source, and read them as a sign that AI companies want to avoid paying for content. The result, he argued, is that models can’t draw on the best material available to them specifically enough and too often fall back on generalities. He called this an early form of enshittification in AI.

O’Reilly takes the opposite position. Andrew explained that the company applies the royalty model it already uses for O’Reilly Answers. Material returned through the Expert MCP server can be cited, and authors are paid royalties on it, so that expert content has a market and earns a return.

In response to an audience question, Tim and Andrew noted that Expert Intelligence is in prerelease with a group of founding partners while O’Reilly works out its economics. Interested organizations can request access through the product page.

Putting the discussion where the AI can see it

The second part of Andrew’s presentation dealt with what happens after the agent writes a report. Decisions need consensus, and with AI-generated analysis people need to check that the model hasn’t keyed off something unimportant, out-of-date, or misinterpreted. “The AI can identify all the trade-offs,” he said, “but people still need to make the decisions that matter.”

His team first circulated reports as Google Docs, but they ran into two problems. The most interesting part of a document under review is usually the comment thread, and because at this time, O’Reilly company policy doesn’t allow MCP connections to Google Docs, the agent couldn’t see it. And when Andrew asked the model to fold the discussion back into the document, pasting the result wiped out the comments.

Doug Hogan, an O’Reilly engineering director, built an alternative on top of Git and GitHub that Andrew called SuperAnswers. (Andrew joked that this was why he isn’t allowed to name things.) Documents live in a Git repository, discussion lives in GitHub Discussions, and every change is versioned. Andrew can ask his agent what the consensus is on a project, have it incorporate comments into a new draft without losing history, and later reconstruct when a decision was made and what people knew at the time. The same record lets him generate the derivative documents a decision requires, such as scope statements for engineering, product, and design teams, or a meeting agenda. A graph view clusters the topics people are discussing and flags decisions that are still open.

Tim summarized the whole system as a research assistant connected to the organization’s sources of truth, a layer of outside expertise to put its findings in context, and a shared, versioned discussion that becomes an evolving store of organizational knowledge, which makes the AI a more useful coworker. Andrew agreed and said he would like to open-source SuperAnswers, which he described as a thin layer on top of Git.

Andrew also pointed out that the fragmentation he was addressing isn’t limited to engineering. Sales teams have their information spread across systems like Salesforce, 6sense, and Gainsight, and every function has the same need to pull those threads together. Tim added that tool access is uneven across the industry and always has been. Claude produces better PowerPoint than Google Slides, Gemini the reverse, and organizations have to capture that kind of knowledge about their own toolsets.

Questions from the audience

An audience member named Thomas worried that workers now talk to AI rather than to each other, and that work disappears into “that AI hole.” Andrew said his preference for keeping everything in Git is partly an answer to that, since it gives both humans and AI a central place to find and reconstruct past work. But his larger interest is in humans talking to humans in a way that AI supports. He described a category of questions he never used to ask:

I knew, if I ask this question, somebody’s got to go off for two weeks and compile all this stuff from all these different systems. Now I can gather it in a few minutes. Maybe some of this is throwaway, but it’s not bad if it’s cheap.

In response to that “throwaway” comment, one audience member wrote in the chat: “This is not throwaway work, Andrew. It is a product lead that changes the value proposition in a positive direction. Shit hot, bro.” Tim couldn’t help but read that one aloud!

Asked by Tim what he got wrong, Andrew conceded that he didn’t think early enough about how people would review and respond to AI-generated documents. People don’t want an AI-generated data dump to wade through, and they extend AI no benefit of the doubt. If an AI-written report gets one small fact wrong about Kubernetes operators, a reader is likely to dismiss the whole document. AI tools have to be understood as marshaling and presenting evidence, not making decisions. “These need to support your analytical capacity, not replace it.”

Tim connected that answer to concerns about deskilling. He described a fine-tuning project he attempted with Fable to train a small model to write more like him. He wanted to understand each stage rather than letting the model run, but it never explained them, and the training run failed. In part this was because the model asked him to provide samples of his writing, but it didn’t give him enough grounding on what a really good training dataset would look like, so the samples weren’t targeted enough. They were too long, and when Fable chose the short fragments it actually needed, it didn’t do an ideal job.

When Tim tried the same project with O’Reilly Tutor, a tool still in development, it sent him to read an O’Reilly resource on what a good training set looks like, and he realized where he went wrong. Tim compared the kind of deskilling that can happen when people just turn the work over to AI to people who can no longer read a map, or who call a plumber for a simple fix they could do themselves in 30 seconds if they only knew a bit more about how things work. He argued that everyone has an obligation to keep learning alongside the tools they use.

An audience member named David, a laid-off engineer looking to reskill, made a similar point. We used to know things, then we searched, and now we skip the search and just ask for the answer. He asked how to build real depth. Andrew suggested picking a project and working through every aspect of it, asking AI to act as a tutor (he’s relearning calculus that way) and keeping a book open alongside, or taking advantage of instructor-led live events on fast-moving topics.

The conversation ended with the difference between an AI system that simply makes an organization faster and one that makes it better at deciding what to do. In Andrew’s account, getting better at deciding what work needs doing depends on three things the models don’t supply on their own: a map of where the organization’s knowledge lives, a body of expertise that people trust, and a place where the humans can argue with what the AI produced.

You can watch full episodes of Live with Tim O’Reilly, including this one, on the O’Reilly learning platform, YouTube, or wherever you get your podcasts.

item.content:encoded:
AI agents dominated the news this week, from security exploits that unfolded in hours to new tools that let agents shop, manage transactions, and conduct scientific research. On the latest episode of This Week in AI, host Vicki Reyzelman of Akamai examined how these developments are testing existing security practices and creating new opportunities for businesses and researchers.

AI attacks are outpacing traditional security responses

AI is changing how attackers find and exploit vulnerabilities. A supply chain attack involving ARTEX, an open source agentic AI penetration-testing framework, helped attackers reach more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants through a ConnectWise compromise. The incident raised concerns about OAuth authentication and the limitations of conventional identity protections when autonomous agents interact with enterprise systems.

A more immediate threat came from PHP2Shell, two vulnerabilities rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale that could allow attackers to execute code on vulnerable web servers without authentication. CISA urged immediate patching following the October 21 disclosure. Researchers also documented attackers using AI agents to obtain password hashes and MFA secrets from a European government system within two hours. The speed of exploitation leaves organizations little time to investigate threats before responding, especially smaller businesses with limited security resources.

Security teams can no longer rely on manual review alone. They need automated detection and response, tighter access controls, and network segmentation to limit what compromised agents can reach. But monitoring autonomous agents is challenging. Researchers from METR and Redwood Research identified weaknesses in an earlier version of OpenAI’s internal monitoring system, including one that could allow hundreds of agent actions to be concealed. OpenAI says it has patched vulnerabilities affecting production safeguards, although the researchers haven’t independently evaluated those changes.

The debate over AI safety is also extending beyond technical safeguards. Anthropic proposed federal AI safety legislation, while Google DeepMind employees resigned over the company’s military AI work. Both developments illustrate the growing pressure on AI companies to establish clearer rules for how their technology is developed and used.

The transition to agents brings new challenges

Retailers are taking different approaches to autonomous shopping. Walmart introduced an Agent Gateway that lets approved agents shop within customer-defined spending limits and approval requirements. Amazon has restricted some third-party shopping agents, while banks including Morgan Stanley and Bank of America are limiting agent access to customer accounts. The disagreement goes beyond security. Retailers that depend on advertising and product recommendations have an incentive to keep shoppers on their websites. As more purchases begin with agents, companies will have to reconsider how they maintain customer relationships.

Anthropic is testing a different approach to agent oversight. Claude’s auto mode is becoming the default for Pro, Max, and Team users, allowing automated checks to approve routine actions and block risky ones. Anthropic also contributed its Agent Skills format to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. More than 70 platforms have adopted the standard, with over a million skills published. Shared formats could make workflows easier to reuse across products, although organizations still need to control which actions those workflows can perform.

Growing agent use also requires more computing capacity and electricity. We discussed NVIDIA’s $164.5 billion in commitments and guarantees supporting AI data centers, including an Ohio campus that SB Energy is building for OpenAI. Power shortages have delayed other projects, including a proposed data center in Essex, where grid operators couldn’t promise adequate electricity until the 2030s. Meanwhile, Amazon is backing a 960-megawatt nuclear project, and Brookfield and NextEra are pursuing a $100 billion AI hub at a former nuclear site in Kentucky. However, money and chips alone can’t solve AI’s infrastructure constraints when electricity generation and grid capacity take years to expand.

AI is accelerating discovery, but validation still takes time

Healthcare offered a more encouraging view of AI’s capabilities. A study of Microsoft’s MAI Diagnostic Orchestrator found that it correctly diagnosed 83.2% of difficult medical cases, compared with 36.1% for generalist physicians. The comparison didn’t include specialists, and the system still needs clinical validation. The research nevertheless suggests AI could help physicians investigate difficult cases and identify conditions they might otherwise miss.

Drug discovery could also benefit from more capable agents. OpenAI announced its acquisition of Orchestra Bio, a platform that coordinates drug development workflows, with plans to integrate it with Rosalind, its life sciences research tools. The combination could help researchers manage experiments and collaborate more efficiently during a development process that typically takes 10 to 15 years from initial discovery to approval.

An Anthropic protein-design experiment provided a concrete example of faster early-stage research. In 64 hours, an Anthropic model generated 318,484 candidate protein designs targeting scorpion venom. Researchers from Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience subsequently tested 211 designs and identified 17 that bound to toxins. The researchers haven’t established whether those proteins can neutralize venom, but the experiment showed how AI can rapidly narrow a vast search space before scientists begin more expensive laboratory testing.

What’s next

We’ll be back on Monday, November 2, for another episode covering the latest developments in AI research and applications. You can catch previous episodes on YouTube, Spotify, Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts.

item.dc:creator: Tim O'Brien
item.custom:subtitle: We need mechanisms that bind an agent’s agency to an approved world model
